frameworks.name: Five Steps to Live the Life You Want
frameworks.definition: A five-stage decision framework: (1) figure out what you want, (2) ignore others' opinions, (3) do so much work it would be unreasonable to fail, (4) realize it never mattered, (5) help others once you get there.

frameworks.name: One More Frame (Permission-Based Change)
frameworks.definition: A mental model that reframes personal changes (relationships, habits, businesses) as temporary one-day commitments rather than permanent decisions, enabling faster action without sunk-cost regret.

claims.text: Figuring out what you want is 99% of success; once you know what you want, getting it is the easy part (Alex Hormozi's first boss).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Clarity transforms opportunity cost calculation—once you know what you truly want, every other option becomes transparent as something you're willing to sacrifice.

claims.text: Permission to change what you want mid-path, without sunk-cost regret, accelerates major life and business pivots. Reframing changes as one-day commitments rather than permanent decisions (the 'one more' frame) removes the weight that blocks decisive action.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Sunk-life bias (treating past investment as reason to continue) is replaced by permission-based framing (I will do X today; tomorrow I will decide again). This decouples action from permanence, enabling faster pivots.

claims.text: Successful people make trades and accept that they cannot have it all; life gives nothing to those unwilling to trade. Most deathbed regrets stem from wanting the benefits of a path they didn't choose without accepting its costs.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Regret emerges from the illusion that you could have had both paths' benefits without either path's costs. Accepting tradeoffs minimizes regret by aligning expectation with choice.
bounded_by: Does not mean all tradeoffs are worthwhile or well-calibrated
Does not eliminate the reality of opportunity cost—only reframes the emotional weight

claims.text: Purpose is stable and internal; passion is fickle and external. The source of motivation (pain, shame, purpose, meaning) does not determine outcomes—only whether the drive is sustained.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Taking action despite discomfort builds confidence retroactively; confidence is not a precondition for courage. Declaring permission for a one-day change is sufficient to move; emotion follows behavior, not the reverse.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Action under discomfort triggers behavioral proof and reinforcement; the completion itself rewires belief. Waiting for confidence pre-action guarantees stasis.

examples.text: Hormozi's first boss told him that figuring out what he wanted was 99% of the problem, and once he knew, getting it would be easy. This frame shaped his approach to every major decision afterward, because clarity on the target transforms the willingness to sacrifice everything else.

When someone says a partner told them to pick up their socks and they immediately think 'she'll nag me forever, I need to break up,' the 'one more' frame (used by Ed Milet for addiction recovery) resets that catastrophizing. Instead: 'I will pick up my socks today. Tomorrow I will decide if I want to continue. If five days from now I decide I need a day off, that's what I need that day—not burnout, just a day.' This permission to renegotiate daily accelerates significant life changes.

A person says they sacrificed family time for career success and now wants it all back. But they chose the career path and didn't sacrifice for family because they weren't willing to pay that cost then. Their regret is not about the path they took—it's about wanting both paths' benefits without either path's price. This confusion between 'could have had both' and 'could have paid for both' is at the heart of most deathbed regrets.

practices.text: Figure out what you want clearly and write it down.
Do so much work on your goal that failure would be unreasonable given the effort level.
Ignore others' opinions about your goal once it is clear.
When facing major life or business changes, grant yourself permission to make the change for one day at a time; do not anchor to permanence.
Help others once you have achieved your own goals.
